Formalized Agent Foundations — the trust-surface read-through

Every paper node beside the Lean statement that carries it, for every paper this repository formalizes. The kernel has already checked every proof body; what it cannot check is whether each statement says what the paper says. That judgment requires a human reader — this page is the map for making it.

What a read-through certifies

A kernel-clean proof certifies that the body matches the statement, and nothing more. The statement — its definitions, hypotheses, and conclusion — is the trust surface. Reading a node means holding the two panes side by side and asking four questions:

1 · Fidelity. Does the Lean statement say what the paper node says — same quantifiers, same conclusion shape, no strengthened premise doing hidden work?
2 · Satisfiability. Is every hypothesis inhabitable? Constructed witnesses are named in the audit notes; a premise with no possible inhabitant makes the theorem vacuously true, and this failure mode has occurred (and been repaired) before.
3 · No smuggling. Is the conclusion (or the forcing step) taken as a hypothesis anywhere? Structures' fields are hypotheses too — see the field-freeze appendices.
4 · Metering. Where a paper's own statement quantifies over an efficiency class, check which class the Lean statement actually uses; the classes are not interchangeable, and the narrower ones appear only where a node is marked qualified.

What is on each card, and what is not

Every card is the same mechanical pair: the paper's printed statement — machine-converted from the committed TeX, or, where no TeX source for the paper exists, shown verbatim as extracted from the committed PDF — beside the exact source text of the Lean statement (or statements) annotated with that node. Beyond that pair, the papers carry different editorial material, because different material exists — and the difference is real, not a presentational choice:

Only Logical Induction has a strength classification and per-node reading notes. They are the product of a dedicated re-derivation pass and a machine-checked table; the other two libraries have had no such pass. No tier, audit note or reading note is shown for a paper that does not have one — the correspondence is what those sections claim, and it is all they claim.

How to use this page

Within each paper, nodes appear in that paper's own order, grouped by its own sections; definitions come first and are load-bearing for everything after. Where a node has several inventory endpoints, the ‹ › arrows page through all of them. Check-boxes track progress across all three papers and persist locally in the browser. Signatures are statements only, verbatim from source; file paths locate the full declaration. Paper statements are machine-converted from the arXiv TeX (custom macros expanded, rendered as MathML) — for any formula that looks off, the arXiv PDF is the authority; the Lean pane is exact source text.

Generated from the repository by scripts/gen-trust-surface.py, driven by the paper registry scripts/papers.py; node locations come from scripts/paper_nodes.py, the same module the per-paper provenance checkers use. The page carries a hash over every input — each paper's source, every library's Lean sources, the registry and the prose files quoted here — and scripts/check_trust_surface.py fails CI if it is stale.

The two standing disclosures (apply to every node)

Sentences are propositional (Formula ℕ); the paper's first-order Θ enters through explicit interfaces. Efficient computability is the fuel-clocked interpreter model dd:fuel, not a machine complexity class. "Paper strength" always means within this disclosed model. Details: LogicalInduction/README.md, "The two modeling boundaries".

Tiers

paper strength · universal31 — the paper's own statement, for every logical inductor
paper strength · instantiated32 — additionally holds of the constructed LIA with obligations discharged
qualified3 — a named interface or class restriction is retained; the note says which

The tier and note on every card are read from scripts/coverage-classification.md, which is machine-checked against the endpoint inventory on every build, so a node cannot ship without a strength call. The qualified rows deserve the slow pass: each one's note names exactly what is retained and why.

Metering vocabulary

RpnSentenceCodes / symbol-metered classes are the faithful rendering of the paper's def:ec; whole-value classes (PolyNatCodes &c.) are provably narrower and appear only where a row is marked qualified.

The Logical Induction Criterion

def:lic The Logical Induction Criterion paper strength · instantiated
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

A market ℙ― is said to satisfy the logical induction criterion relative to a deductive process D― if there is no efficiently computable trader T that exploits ℙ― relative to D―. A market ℙ― meeting this criterion is called a logical inductor over D―.

Lean · statement only (proof body is kernel-checked)
IsLogicalInductorLogicalInduction/Framework/Criterion.lean
class IsLogicalInductor (P : History) (DP : DeductiveProcess) : Prop where
  /-- Markets are computable rational pricing sequences in the paper's definition. -/
  marketComputable : ComputableMarket P
  /-- Deductive processes are computable nested finite-set sequences in the paper's
  definition. -/
  processComputable : ComputableDeductiveProcess DP
  /-- No efficiently computable trader exploits `P`. -/
  noExploit : ∀ Tr : Trader, EfficientlyComputable Tr → ¬ Tr.Exploits P DP
How the panes line up The class bundles the criterion (noExploit, quantified over EfficientlyComputable traders) with two facts the paper leaves ambient: the market and the process are computable. P n φ is the paper's ℙₙ(φ).
What to check range law bundled through marketComputable; trader class is def:ec's, disclosed globally

codeEvalnNat_polyFueledLogicalInduction/Framework/Emission.lean
lemma codeEvalnNat_polyFueled :
    ∀ c : Nat.Partrec.Code, ∃ prog, PolyFueled prog (codeEvalnNat c)
  | .zero =>
    (polyFueled_baseGuard (PolyFueled.const 0)).imp fun _ h =>
      h.of_eq fun z => (codeEvalnNat_zero_eq z).symm
  | .succ =>
    (polyFueled_baseGuard PolyFueled.right.succ_comp).imp fun _ h =>
      h.of_eq fun z => (codeEvalnNat_succ_eq z).symm
  | .left =>
    (polyFueled_baseGuard (PolyFueled.left.comp PolyFueled.right)).imp fun _ h =>
      h.of_eq fun z => (codeEvalnNat_left_eq z).symm
  | .right =>
    (polyFueled_baseGuard (PolyFueled.right.comp PolyFueled.right)).imp fun _ h =>
      h.of_eq fun z => (codeEvalnNat_right_eq z).symm
  | .pair cf cg =>
    codeEvalnNat_pair_polyFueled (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cf) (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cg)
  | .comp cf cg =>
    codeEvalnNat_comp_polyFueled (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cf) (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cg)
  | .prec cf cg =>
    codeEvalnNat_prec_polyFueled (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cf) (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cg)
  | .rfind' cf =>
    codeEvalnNat_rfind_polyFueled (codeEvalnNat_polyFueled cf)

/-! ## The bounded dovetail

The paper's `app:prandaff` clock is built from an *arbitrary-runtime* decider run under a
growing budget:

> `DefinitelySettled(n, m) :↔ ∃ i ≤ m: settled(n, i)` returns true within `m` steps

with the three properties it needs: poly in `m`; `DefinitelySettled → Settled`; and if
`Settled(n,m)` then `DefinitelySettled(n,M)` for some `M ≥ m`.  Nothing here is specific to
settlement — this is the generic move that turns *any* code into a polynomial Boolean table
that is monotone in the budget and eventually fires.  It is what
`PatientSettlementClock.active_codes` (`Properties/Pseudorandomness.lean`) and
`HistoricalVerifiedMaturitySchedule.check_poly` (`Framework/ROI.lean`) both need, so it is
stated once, generically.

The simulator (`codeEvalnNat_polyFueled`) is what makes the budgeted run polynomial;
`polyFueled_boundedAny` supplies the bounded search. -/

/-- `c` returns `1` on input `x` within `fuel` steps of the clocked interpreter.
(`codeEvalnNat` normalizes `none ↦ 0` and `some out ↦ out+1`, so acceptance is `2`.) -/
def acceptsWithin (c : Nat.Partrec.Code) (fuel x : ℕ) : Bool

Traders

def:tradestrat Trading Strategy paper strength · instantiated
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

A trading strategy for day n, also called an n-strategy, is an affine combination of the form

T=c+ξ1ϕ1+⋯+ξkϕk,
where ϕ1,…,ϕk are sentences, ξ1,…,ξk are expressible features of rank ≤n, and
c=−∑iξi*nϕi
is a “cash term” recording the net cash flow when executing a transaction that buys ξi shares of ϕi for each i at the prevailing market price. (Buying negative shares is called “selling”.) We define T[1] to be c, and T[ϕ] to be the coefficient of ϕ in T, which is 0 if ϕ∉(ϕ1,…,ϕk). An n-strategy T can be encoded by the tuples (ϕ1,…ϕk) and (ξ1,…ξk) because the c term is determined by them. Explicitly, by linearity we have
T=ξ1·(ϕ1−*nϕ1)+⋯+ξk·(ϕk−*nϕk),
which means any n-strategy can be written as a linear combination of (ϕi−*nϕi) terms, each of which means “buy one share of ϕi at the prevailing price”.

Lean · statement only (proof body is kernel-checked)
StrategyLogicalInduction/Framework/Criterion.lean
structure Strategy (n : ℕ) where
  /-- The `(expressible-feature coefficient, sentence)` pairs `(eᵢ, φᵢ)`. -/
  trades : List (EF × Sentence)
  /-- Every coefficient has rank `≤ n` (the strategy sees only prices up to day `n`). -/
  rank_le : ∀ p ∈ trades, p.1.rank ≤ n
How the panes line up trades is the affine combination (the paper's ξ₁φ₁+…); rank_le is the paper's rank condition — an n-strategy mentions only prices of days ≤ n.
What to check direct rendering, with the paper's rank/horizon bound on traded features

def:affcomsen Affine Combination paper strength · instantiated
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

An ℱ-combination A:𝒮∪{1}→ℱ is an affine expression of the form

A:=c+α1ϕ1+⋯+αkϕk,
where (ϕ1,…,ϕk) are sentences and (c,α1,…,αk) are in ℱ. We define ℝ-combinations, ℚ-combinations, and EF-combinations analogously. We write A[1] for the trailing coefficient c, and A[ϕ] for the coefficient of ϕ, which is 0 if ϕ∉(ϕ1,…,ϕk). The rank of A is defined to be the maximum rank among all its coefficients. Given any valuation 𝕍, we abuse notation in the usual way and define the value of A (according to 𝕍) linearly by:
𝕍(A):=c+α1𝕍(ϕ1)+⋯+αk𝕍(ϕk).
An ℱ-combination progression is a sequence A― of affine combinations where An has rank ≤n. An EF-combination progression is defined similarly.

thm:lc Limit Coherence paper strength · universal
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

ℙ∞ is coherent, i.e., it gives rise to an internally consistent probability measure Pr on the set PC(Γ) of all worlds consistent with Γ, defined by the formula

Pr(𝕎(ϕ)=1):=ℙ∞(ϕ).
In particular, if Γ contains the axioms of first-order logic, then ℙ∞ defines a probability measure on the set of first-order completions of Γ.

Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

Let ϕ― be an e.c. sequence of decidable sentences, a and b be rational numbers, δ― be an e.c. sequence of positive rational numbers, and suppose that ∑n(Indδi(a<ℙi(ϕi)<b))i∈ℕ+=∞. Then, if the sequence

    (P : History) (DP : DeductiveProcess) [IsLogicalInductor P DP]
    (φ : ℕ → Sentence) (truth : ℕ → ℝ)

def:deferralfunc Deferral Function paper strength · instantiated
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

A function f:ℕ+→ℕ+ is called a deferral function if

  1. f(n)>n for all n, and
  2. f(n) can be computed in time polynomial in f(n), i.e., if there is some algorithm and a polynomial function h such that for all n, the algorithm computes f(n) within h(f(n)) steps.
If f is a deferral function, we say that f defers n to f(n).

Lean · statement only (proof body is kernel-checked)
DeferralFunctionLogicalInduction/Properties/SelfTrust.lean
structure DeferralFunction where
  /-- The underlying function. -/
  f : ℕ → ℕ
  /-- `f` defers: `f n > n`. -/
  lt : ∀ n, n < f n
  /-- A code computing `f`. -/
  code : Nat.Partrec.Code
  /-- The code halts within fuel polynomial in `f n`. -/
  fueled : ∃ a k : ℕ, ∀ n,
    Nat.Partrec.Code.evaln (a * (f n + 1) ^ k + a) code n = some (f n)
How the panes line up lt is f(n) > n; fueled renders “f computable in time polynomial in f(n)” as a poly clock in the output, exactly as the paper demands (so f may grow fast).
What to check direct rendering: n < f n with the emitter clocked polynomially in f n, as the paper asks

UPrefix.UHalt_functionalLogicalInduction/Construction/Witnesses/UniversalPrefix.lean
lemma UHalt_functional : ∀ (v : List Bool) (y y' : ℕ), UHalt v y → UHalt v y' → y = y'
  | [], _, _, h, _ => absurd h (by simp [UHalt])
  | false :: _, _, _, h, h' => by
      rw [UHalt_builtin] at h h'; rw [h] at h'; exact Option.some_injective _ h'
  | [true], _, _, h, _ => absurd h (by simp [UHalt])
  | true :: false :: v, _, _, h, h' => by
      obtain ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
UPrefix.acc_antichainLogicalInduction/Construction/Witnesses/UniversalPrefix.lean
lemma acc_antichain : ∀ (t : ℕ) (p q : ℕ × List Bool), p ∈ acc t → q ∈ acc t →
    p.1 = q.1 → p.2 <+: q.2 → p = q
  | 0 => by simp [acc]
  | t + 1 => by
      intro p q hp hq hcode hpre
      rw [acc] at hp hq
      by_cases h : accOK t (acc t)
      · rw [if_pos h] at hp hq
        rcases List.mem_cons.mp hp with rfl | hp' <;> rcases List.mem_cons.mp hq with rfl | hq'
        · rfl
        · exact absurd hpre (accOK_guard h hq' hcode.symm).2
        · exact absurd hpre (accOK_guard h hp' hcode).1
        · exact acc_antichain t p q hp' hq' hcode hpre
      · rw [if_neg h] at hp hq
        exact acc_antichain t p q hp hq hcode hpre

thm:dus Domination of the Universal Semimeasure paper strength · universal
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

Let (b1,b2,…) be a sequence of zero-arity predicate symbols in ℒ not mentioned in Γ, and let σ≤n=(σ1,…,σn) be any finite bitstring. Define

ℙ∞(σ≤n):=ℙ∞(“(b1⟺σ1―=1)∧(b2⟺σ2―=1)∧…∧(bn⟺σn―=1)”),
such that, for example, ℙ∞(01101)=ℙ∞(“¬b1∧b2∧b3∧¬b4∧b5”). Let M be a universal continuous semimeasure. Then there is some positive constant C such that for any finite bitstring σ≤n,
ℙ∞(σ≤n)≥C·M(σ≤n).

where the nth pricing is conditioned on the first n sentences in ψ―, is a logical inductor over Γ∪{ψi∣i∈ℕ+}.

def:luv Logically Uncertain Variable paper strength · instantiated
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

A logically uncertain variable, abbreviated LUV, is any formula X free in one variable that defines a unique value via Γ, in the sense that

Γ⊢∃x:(X(x)∧∀x′:X(x′)→x′=x).
We refer to that value as the value of X. If Γ proves that the value of X is in [0,1], we call X a [0,1]-LUV.

Given a [0,1]-LUV X and a consistent world 𝕎∈PC(Γ), the value of X in 𝕎 is defined to be

𝕎(X):=sup{x∈[0,1]∣𝕎(“X≥x―”)=1}.
In other words, 𝕎(X) is the supremum of values that do not exceed X according to 𝕎. (This rather roundabout definition is necessary in cases where 𝕎 assigns X a non-standard value.)

We write 𝒰 for the set of all [0,1]-LUVs. When manipulating logically uncertain variables, we use shorthand like “X<0.5” for “∀x:X(x)→x<0.5”. See Secnotation for details.

𝔼∞(X):=limn→∞𝔼n(X)
exists for all X∈𝒰.

thm:loe Linearity of Expectation paper strength · universal

Let a―,b― be bounded ℙ‾-generable sequences of rational numbers, and let X―,Y―, and Z― be e.c. sequences of [0,1]-LUVs. If we have Γ⊢Zn=anXn+bnYn for all n, then

an𝔼n(Xn)+bn𝔼n(Yn)≈n𝔼n(Zn).

How the panes line up hval is exactly tex's premise: a one-sided bound on the combination's value over completed worlds, each world free to choose its own valuation ν. The paper's ≳/≲/≈ statement appears as the _ge/_le/_eq trio.
What to check lic_expect_combination_provind_ge/_le/_eq now take exactly tex:1753-1760's premise — a one-sided bound ∀ v, v.ConsistentWithTheory DP → ∀ ν, (As n).ValuesAt v ν → c ≤ (As n).value P ν over cworlds(Θ), with completed worlds free to disagree. DeterminedViaTheory is gone from them; the determinacy forms survive as _ofDetermined corollaries because thm:recurringunbiasednessexp/thm:wubexp/thm:prandexp genuinely take that premise (def:affthmval). WorldValued is retained and is the paper's own representation premise — operationally it is what produces the valuation ν the bound is stated against. Note the fixed-LUV endpoints lic_expectation_provind_ofValuesAt still quantify over stage-consistent worlds; they are a separate rendering, not this node's paper statement

Let B―∈BLCS(ℙ―). Then

lim infn→∞inf𝕎∈PC(Γ)𝕎(Bn)≤lim infn→∞𝔼∞(Bn)≤lim infn→∞𝔼n(Bn),
and

thm:recurringunbiasednessexp Expectation Recurring Unbiasedness paper strength · universal
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

If B―∈BLCS(ℙ―) is determined via Γ, and w― is a ℙ‾-generable divergent weighting weighting such that the support of w― is contained in the image of f,

∑i≤nwi·(𝔼i(Bi)−ValΓ(Bi))∑i≤nwi
has 0 as a limit point. In particular, if it converges, it converges to 0.

thm:wubexp Expectation Unbiasedness From Feedback paper strength · instantiated
Paper · arXiv:1609.03543v5

Given B―∈BLCS(ℙ―) that is determined via Γ, a strictly increasing deferral function f such that ValΓ(An) can be computed in time 𝒪(f(n+1)), and a ℙ‾-generable divergent weighting w,

∑i≤nwi·(𝔼i(Bi)−ValΓ(Bi))∑i≤nwi≈n0.
In this case, we say “w― allows good feedback on B―”.

How the panes line up Exact zero-slack endpoint over one non-vacuous canonical process fixed from T. A fixed old-language lift and executable finite-entailment gate internally admit every arbitrary e.c. source satisfying the paper's completed-world [0,1]-valued premise; deferred weight, exact product, and right quotation are constructed internally.
What to check lic_no_expected_net_update_conditional_closed_exact takes exactly the paper-facing source interface (X : ℕ → LUV, RpnThresholdCodeSeq X, and completed-world source_valued), a bare DeferralFunction, and a P-generable [0,1] weight. A fixed atom injection represents the caller's source in an old-language namespace, and a universal finite-entailment gate derives source admission from source_valued; no freshness or proof-carrying certificate is caller-visible. The sole market is liaHistory (canonicalCCEEDP T), whose computable, explicitly non-vacuous process is fixed from T before X, f, or w. Deferred-weight and right-hand quotation LUVs are built internally, semantic multiplication is exact, and the generic CCEE theorem is instantiated with identically zero slack. This is one canonical enlarged language from the outset, not a source-dependent extension and not a market-correspondence claim about liaHistory (theoremDP T).

Cartesian Frames

Garrabrant, Herrmann, Lopez-Wild (2021) · arXiv:2109.10996v1 · CartesianFrames/ · 60 nodes

No strength classification exists for this paper. There is no per-node tier and no per-node audit note below, because neither has been produced: the dedicated re-derivation pass and the machine-checked strength table that Logical Induction has were never run here. What the cards below assert is the correspondence — this printed node, these Lean statements — and nothing about how strong each rendering is. Read the statements.

Scope

All 60 numbered nodes of the paper carry Lean statements, across the main text and both appendices, with no modeling substitutions. Numbered nodes with no Lean statement: none — every numbered node of the paper has a Lean statement. One node is formalized only in part, by user ruling — its card says so, in the ruling's own words.

How nodes are cited

Most nodes of this paper carry no LaTeX \label, so the printed Definition n / Claim n / Theorem n is the provenance key. scripts/check-cartesian-frames-nodes.py validates every annotation against the committed TeX fail-closed, and requires each annotated declaration to be listed in AxiomAudit.lean's CF-INVENTORY block. The cards below are built from those same annotations, so a node's Lean pane shows exactly the declarations that claim it.

Where the printed proof is the thing that is wrong

Defects found in this paper during formalization are recorded in CartesianFrames/notes/paper-errata.md; a node with an erratum carries it on its card. Consult it before concluding that a Lean proof diverges from the printed one — in several places the statement is sound and the printed proof is not.

Inventoried endpoints that carry no annotation

Not every axiom-checked endpoint of this library renders a numbered node. The inventory's own preamble, quoted verbatim from AxiomAudit.lean:

Same contract as the Logical Induction inventory above, for CartesianFrames/ (paper: arXiv:2109.10996). Most of that paper's nodes carry no LaTeX \label, so Paper node: lines cite the printed Definition n / Claim n / Theorem n numbers; scripts/check-cartesian-frames-nodes.py validates them against the committed TeX and checks that every declaration annotated in the library is itself listed between the CF-INVENTORY markers below — sharing a node with a listed declaration is not enough. Five groups of listed names carry no annotation of their own: the constructive carriers of Appendix B's Claims 46 and 48 (Frame.dualEquivalence, Frame.zeroIsInitial, Frame.topIsTerminal — the theorems state the paper's propositional content, these are the data behind them); the four unnumbered facts the paper uses silently (Frame.Biextensional.nonempty_iso_collapse, the step taken whenever a biextensional frame is replaced by its collapse, together with the three ≃ᵇ-invariants Frame.image_eq_of_biextEquiv, Frame.exists_env_injective_of_biextEquiv — the standard refuters for ◁ₓ and ◁₊ — and Frame.BiextEquiv.dual, which every dualized definition runs on); the inhabitation of Definition 31's choice functions (Frame.partitionSectionsOut and the Nonempty instance built from it, which the paper assumes without comment); the one combined-iff convenience wrapper (Frame.addSubagent_iff_addSubagentCategorical, whose two halves are the annotated Claims 55 and 56); and the last three blocks, the non-vacuity, subagency, and operation/Appendix-B witnesses of CartesianFrames/Examples.lean, listed here so that the separations they assert are axiom-checked alongside the definitions they constrain.

Definition 2 definition
Paper · arXiv:2109.10996v1

A morphism from C=(A,E,·) to D=(B,F,⋆) is a pair of functions (g:A→B,h:F→E) satisfying a·h(f)=g(a)⋆f for all a∈A,f∈F. We call this equation the adjointness condition for morphisms. For two morphisms (g0,h0),(g1,h1), their composition is given by (g1,h1)∘(g0,h0)=(g1∘g0,h0∘h1).

Definition 4 definition
Paper · arXiv:2109.10996v1

A Cartesian frame C=(A,E,·) is called biextensional if whenever a0,a1∈A are such that a0·e=a1·e for all e∈E, then a0=a1, and whenever e0,e1∈E are such that a·e0=a·e1 for all a∈A, then e0=e1.

  env_ext : ∀ ⦃e₀ e₁ : C.Env⦄, (∀ a, C.outcome a e₀ = C.outcome a e₁) → e₀ = e₁
Definition 5 definition
Paper · arXiv:2109.10996v1

Given a Cartesian frame C=(A,E,·), for a0,a1∈A, we say a0~a1 if a0·e=a1·e for all e∈E. For e0,e1∈E, we say e0~e1 if a·e0=a·e1 for all a∈A.

Then for a∈A, let a^ denote the equivalence class of a up to ~. Let A^ denote the set of equivalence classes of ~ in A. Similarly, let e^ denote the equivalence class of e up to ~, and let E^ denote the set of equivalence classes of ~ in E.

Intentional deviation (user ruling) Claim 35, External/Internal half: not formalized (Anson, 2026-08-11). The half is ill-typed in the paper's own set theory: External^B(C) has agent A/B, and B is a partition of A, not of A/B, so External^B(External^B(C)) is not well-formed as written; likewise Internal. The claim's binder line also garbles indices (Assume^B with B ⊆ A; External^F with F a partition of E, contradicting Definition 32). Ruling: record as a paper erratum (notes/paper-errata.md #3) and formalize only the Commit/Assume half of Claim 35 (at canonical-iso strength per dd:eq-to-iso). The External/Internal half stays unformalized; its idempotence-theorem carriers do not exist and must not be invented. Consequence for the surface accounting: Claim 35 is partially formalized by design — its Paper node: annotation sits only on the Commit/Assume idempotence theorems, and the README discloses the partial status. Auditors: do not raise the missing External/Internal half as a gap; do flag any attempt to formalize it without a new user ruling.

Definition 37 Homotopy equivalence definition
Paper · arXiv:2109.10996v1

C is homotopy equivalent to D, written C≃D, if there exists a pair of morphisms ϕ:C→D, ψ:D→C, such that ψ∘ϕ is homotopic to the identity on C, and ϕ∘ψ is homotopic to the identity on D.

One can view homotopy equivalence as a weakening of isomorphism. If ϕ and ψ composed to equal the identity in both orders, then C and D would be isomorphic. Instead we only require that their compositions are homotopic to the identity in both orders. As it turns out, homotopy equivalence and isomorphism coincide for biextensional frames.

Robust Cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma

Barász, Christiano, Fallenstein, Herreshoff, LaVictoire, Yudkowsky (2014) · arXiv:1401.5577 · ModalAgents/ · 12 nodes

No strength classification exists for this paper. As with Cartesian Frames, the cards below carry no tier and no per-node audit note, because none has been produced. They assert the correspondence only.

Scope — and what is deliberately absent

The cooperation results are carried at the Gödel–Löb level; the §1 and §4 nodes that quantify over arbitrary agents are carried at the arithmetic level they are printed at, so CliqueBot and its separation from the modal agents are in scope. Node-completeness is still not claimed. The nodes with no Lean statement annotated to them, computed from the source and the annotations: Theorem 4.6. That is Theorem 4.6, on modal agents that may refer to their own action — a genuine gap, and the only numbered node of the paper with no Lean statement (see ModalAgents/README.md). The provenance checker deliberately does not check the converse direction, so this page asserts nothing further about it.

How nodes are cited

The paper labels only 22 of its nodes and leaves several formalized ones unlabeled, so the provenance key is the printed number, recomputed from the committed TeX by emulating the paper's shared section-scoped theorem counter (scripts/check-modal-agents-nodes.py). Note that the paper's definition environment is an uncounted trivlist: this paper numbers no definitions at all, so no definition can be cited and none appears below. The definitional content — modal agents, the four concrete agents — lives in Lean declarations attached to the theorems that use them.

Theorem 4.2 Modal fixed point theorem theorem
Paper · arXiv:1401.5577

Suppose that the formula φ(p,q1,…,qn) in the language of GL is modalized in p. Then there is a modal formula ψ(q1,…,qn) such that

GL⊢ψ(q1,…,qn)↔φ(ψ(q1,…,qn),q1,…,qn).
Moreover, if φ is modalized in qi, then so is ψ.

Temporal Inference with Finite Factored Sets

Garrabrant (2021) · arXiv:2109.11513 · FiniteFactoredSets/ · 87 nodes

This formalization is complete for its ruled scope, and no strength classification exists for this paper. The cards below cover §2 through §7 — partitions and factorizations, the chimera function, generation and history, orthogonality and time, subpartitions and conditional orthogonality, characteristic polynomials and their factorization, the fundamental theorem, temporal inference from orthogonality databases including both worked examples, and §7's embedded observations, counterfactability and conditional time. All 96 in-scope nodes are accounted for: 87 carry a Lean declaration of this project's and the remaining nine are rendered outright by Mathlib vocabulary (listed below), so 87 + 9 = 96. Two things are deliberately not claimed, and both are rulings rather than gaps: Conjecture 1 (§7.2) is stated as a Prop and deliberately not proved — no declaration anywhere in the library has that type — and Examples 3 and 4 are out of scope, both concerning infinite factored sets, which is the case the paper itself expects the fundamental theorem to fail in. The cards carry no tier and no per-node audit note, because none has been produced; they assert the correspondence only. Nodes with no Lean statement annotated to them: 9 of the paper’s definitions; 2 of the paper’s examples.

How nodes are cited

The paper carries only 32 \label commands, two of which are not on numbered nodes at all (one labels a table, one labels a section), so exactly 30 of its 98 numbered nodes are labelled — and the labels it does carry are working names (templabel1, templabel2), so the provenance key is the printed number, recomputed from the committed TeX (scripts/check-finite-factored-sets-nodes.py). Unlike the other counter-derived paper here, this one declares each environment without a [section] argument and without sharing counters, so every environment numbers independently and never resets: Definition 1…Definition 50 run the length of the paper alongside Proposition 1…Proposition 36. Note also that the source declares a lemma environment it never uses and a second lemma2 that also prints "Lemma" and carries all three printed Lemmas; the checker fails closed on that ambiguity rather than guessing.

Nodes rendered by Mathlib vocabulary rather than by a declaration

Nine nodes have no Lean carrier of this project's, because the modeling decisions in FiniteFactoredSets.lean render them with vocabulary Mathlib already has. Six are in §2.1: Definition 1 (the disjoint union ⊔S) is absorbed into Setoid and the dependent product, Definition 2 (partition) is Setoid, Definition 5 (∼_X) is the setoid relation, Definition 6 (finer) is ≤, Definition 7 (Dis_S/Ind_S) is ⊥/⊤, and Definition 9 (∏(B)) is the dependent product. The other three are outside §2.1: §5.1's Definition 29 (evaluation p(f)) is MvPolynomial.eval and Definition 30 (support supp(p)) is MvPolynomial.vars; §6.1's Definition 39 (preimages) is Set.preimage, with Setoid.comap for the partition clause. They are recorded in FiniteFactoredSets/README.md rather than inventoried, because there is no declaration of this project's to axiom-check.

Four nodes carried only in part

Four cards pair a whole printed node with a Lean statement covering part of it, on purpose, because the remaining clause is Mathlib's vocabulary rather than a declaration of this project's. Each is recorded in FiniteFactoredSets/README.md's table of Mathlib-rendered nodes.

  • Proposition 2, first sentence. bot_le_and_le_top carries the Proposition 2 annotation but states only that proposition's second sentence — the Dis_S / Ind_S bounds. Its first sentence, that the order is a partial order on Part(S), is Mathlib's PartialOrder (Setoid S) instance.
  • Definition 8, second sentence. The set form ⋁_S(C) is commonRefinement; the binary X ∨_S Y is Mathlib's X ⊓ Y, which is how §3 onward states it. The identification of the two is commonRefinement_pair, a bridge lemma rather than a node carrier.
  • Definition 15, third sentence. "Finite" and "finite-dimensional" factored sets are not a definition this library makes: under dd:finiteness-minimal they are the typeclass hypotheses [Finite S] and Finite F.B, carried on the individual statements that consume them.
  • Proposition 31's word "irreducible." The proposition itself is carried (irreducible_poly_of_mem_irr); it is the meaning of the word that is Mathlib's Irreducible, which over ℝ is strictly stronger than the paper's phrasing and agrees with it on every case the proposition asserts.

One inverted convention, stated once

The paper's order glyphs run opposite to Mathlib's: it writes X ≥_S Y for "X is finer than Y", so the paper's ≥_S is Mathlib's ≤ on Setoid, and Definition 8's common refinement ⋁_S(C) — a join in the paper's notation — is Mathlib's sInf. The Lean statements use Mathlib's convention throughout and never introduce the paper's glyphs, so no statement has to be read under two conventions at once. When comparing a card's paper statement against its Lean statement, this is the one place the two will look like they disagree when they do not.

Factorizations

Definition 10 factorization definition
Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

A factorization of a set S is a set B⊆Part(S) of nontrivial partitions of S such that the function π:S→⨅(B), given by π(s)=(b↦(b,[s]b)), is a bijection.

Proposition 4 proposition
Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

Fix F=(S,B), a factored set, C,D⊆B, and s,t,r∈S.

  1. χCF(s,t)~cs for all c∈C.
  2. χCF(s,t)~bt for all b∈B⧵C.
  3. χCF(s,s)=s.
  4. χB⧵CF(s,t)=χCF(t,s).
  5. χC∪DF(s,t)=χCF(s,χDF(s,t)).
  6. χC∩DF(s,t)=χCF(χDF(s,t),t).
  7. χCF(χCF(s,t),r)=χCF(s,χCF(t,r))=χCF(s,r).
  8. χCF(s,χDF(t,r))=χDF(χCF(s,t),χCF(s,r)).
  9. χCF(χDF(s,t),r)=χDF(χCF(s,r),χCF(t,r)).
  10. χBF(s,t)=s.
  11. χ{}F(s,t)=t.

theorem chimera_spec (C D : Set (Setoid S)) (s t r : S) :
    (∀ c ∈ C, c ∈ F.B → c (F.chimera C s t) s) ∧
    (∀ b ∈ F.B, b ∉ C → b (F.chimera C s t) t) ∧
    F.chimera C s s = s ∧
    F.chimera (F.B \ C) s t = F.chimera C t s ∧
    F.chimera (C ∪ D) s t = F.chimera C s (F.chimera D s t) ∧
    F.chimera (C ∩ D) s t = F.chimera C (F.chimera D s t) t ∧
    (F.chimera C (F.chimera C s t) r = F.chimera C s r ∧
      F.chimera C s (F.chimera C t r) = F.chimera C s r) ∧
    F.chimera C s (F.chimera D t r)
      = F.chimera D (F.chimera C s t) (F.chimera C s r) ∧
    F.chimera C (F.chimera D s t) r
      = F.chimera D (F.chimera C s r) (F.chimera C t r) ∧
    F.chimera F.B s t = s ∧
    F.chimera ∅ s t = t

Proposition 9 proposition
Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

Let F be a finite factored set.

Generating a Partition with Factors

Proposition 10 proposition
Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

Let F=(S,B) be a finite factored set, let X∈Part(S) be a partition of S, and let C be a subset of B. The following are equivalent:

  1. C⊢FX.
  2. χCF(x,S)=x for all x∈X.
  3. χCF(x,S)⊆x for all x∈X.
  4. χCF(x,y)⊆x for all x,y∈X.
  5. χCF(s,t)∈[s]X for all s,t∈S.
  6. χCF(s,t)~Xs for all s,t∈S.
  7. X≤S⋁S(C).

Proposition 11 proposition
Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

Let F=(S,B) be a finite factored set, let C and D be subsets of B, and let X,Y∈Part(S) be partitions of S.

  1. If X≤SY and C⊢FY, then C⊢FX.
  2. If C⊢FX and C⊢FY, then C⊢FX∨SY.
  3. B⊢FX.
  4. {}⊢FX if and only if X=IndS.
  5. If C⊆D and C⊢FX, then D⊢FX.
  6. If C⊢FX and D⊢FX, then C∩D⊢FX.

Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

Let F=(S,B) be a finite factored set, and let X,Y,Z∈Part(S) be partitions of S.

Theorem 2 theorem
Paper · arXiv:2109.11513

Let F=(S,B) be a finite factored set, and let X,Y,Z,W∈Part(S) be partitions of S.

  1. If X⟂FY∣Z, then Y⟂FX∣Z. (symmetry)
  2. If X⟂F(Y∨SW)∣Z, then X⟂FY∣Z and X⟂FW∣Z. (decomposition)
  3. If X⟂F(Y∨SW)∣Z, then X⟂FY∣(Z∨SW). (weak union)
  4. If X⟂FY∣Z and X⟂FW∣(Z∨SY), then X⟂F(Y∨SW)∣Z. (contraction)
  5. If X⟂FY∣Z and X⟂FW∣Z, then X⟂F(Y∨SW)∣Z. (composition)

Garrabrant, Mayer, Wache, Lang, Eisenstat, Dell (2024) · arXiv:2412.02579 · FactoredSpaces/ · 50 nodes

How nodes are cited

The paper labels 45 of its 50 numbered nodes and leaves five unlabeled — among them Definition 4.2, the factored space itself — so the provenance key is the printed number, recomputed from the committed TeX (scripts/check-factored-spaces-nodes.py). The source declares one section-scoped counter shared by theorem, definition, lemma, proposition and corollary (so numbers read Lemma 4.7, Definition 6.1), wraps several results in thmtools' restatable — counted where first stated, not where restated — and letters its appendix sections, so appendix nodes read Lemma A.1, Definition C.6.

Reading the statements

The factored space Ω = ×i∈I Ωi is the dependent function type Pt Ω; the paper's product CJ × CI∖J is stated literally (prodSplit) and worked with through its proved equivalent, closure under splicing two points at J (Finset.piecewise). The design decisions are tagged dd: in FactoredSpaces.lean.

Factored space models

Definition 4.1 Derived Variable definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let X:Ω→Val(X) and Y:Ω→Val(Y) be two random variables, and let C⊆Ω be an event. Then, we say that emphY is derived from X on C, or that it is a deterministic function of X on C if there is a function f:Val(X)→Val(Y), such that for all ω∈C, it holds that Y(ω)=f(X(ω)). We also write this as X▷CY. We write X▷Y as a shorthand for X▷ΩY, and say that Y is derived from X or a deterministic function of X.

Factored spaces and factored space models

Definition 4.2 Factored Space definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

A finite sample space Ω is called a factored space if there is a finite emphindex set I and finite sets Ωi for all i∈I such that \(Omg = timesOmg\) holds. The sets Ωi are called the factors of Ω. Moreover, the random variables Ui:Ω→Ωi with Ui(ω)=πi(ω) are called the background variables of Ω, and we write U=(Ui)i∈I.

Definition 4.4 Factored Space Model definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let Obs be a finite set and let P be a distribution on Obs. Furthermore, let O:Ω→Obs be a random variable on a factored space Ω. Then we say that the tuple ℳ≔(Ω,O) is a emphfactored space model for P if there is a distribution PΩ that factorizes over Ω and satisfies PΩ(O=o)=P(o) for all o∈Obs.

Structural independence

Definition 4.10 Structural Independence definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let X, Y, and Z be random variables in a factored space Ω. Then, X and Y are structurally independent in Ω, denoted as X⟂ΩY, if ℋ(X)∩ℋ(Y)=∅. Moreover, X and Y are emphstructurally independent given Z, denoted as X⟂ΩY∣Z, if we have

ℋ(X∣z)∩ℋ(Y∣z)=∅ for all z∈Val(Z).

Graphoid and semigraphoid axioms

Definition 5.1 Compositional Semigraphoid definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

A semigraphoid is a set of triplets (X,Y,Z), usually denoted as X⟂Y∣Z, that satisfy the symmetry, decomposition, weak union, and contraction axioms, as listed in [ref]. A graphoid citepearl2022graphoids is a semigraphoid that also satisfies the intersection axiom. A compositional graphoid or semigraphoid additionally satisfies the composition axiom.

Definition 5.7 Perfect map definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let G be a DAG with nodes V and value space Val(X). Further, let ℳ=(Ω,O) be a factored space model. Let P be a distribution over some observation space Obs. Then we say that

  1. G is a perfect map of P if Val(X)=Obs and for all sets of nodes V1,V2,V3⊆V, the sets V1 and V2 are d-separated given V3 in G if and only if XV1 and XV2 are independent given XV3 in P.
  2. ℳ is a perfect map of P with regard to a family of variables X=(Xw)w∈W with Xw:Ω→Obs if ℳ is a factored space model of P and for all sets of variables XW1,XW2,XW3⊆X, we have that XW1 and XW2 are independent given XW3 in P if and only if XW1 and XW2 are structurally independent given XW3 in Ω.

Definition 6.1 definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let P be a probability distribution over a sample space Ω, and let A,B,C⊆Ω be events. We say that A and B are independent given C, denoted A⟂⟂PB∣C, if the following holds: beginalign P(A∩ C)P(B∩ C)=P(A∩ B∩ C)P(C)\,. endalign If x,y,z are values of the random variables X,Y,Z, then we write x⟂⟂Py∣z if P(x,z)P(y,z)=P(x,y,z)P(z) holds. For random variables X,Y,Z, we write X⟂⟂PY∣Z if x⟂⟂Py∣z holds for all values x,y,z of X,Y,Z.

Main theorem

Theorem 6.2 Soundness and Completeness of Structural Independence theorem
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let X,Y,Z be random variables on a factored space Ω=⨉i∈IΩi. Then the following statements are equivalent.

  1. X and Y are structurally independent given Z in Ω.
  2. X⟂⟂PY∣Z holds for all probability distributions P that factorize over Ω.

Lemma C.4 Alternative characterization of generation lemma
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let Ω=⨉i∈IΩi be a factored space, let A,C⊆Ω, let J⊆I be a set with complement J―=I⧵J, and suppose that J disintegrates C. The following statements are equivalent:

  1. J generates A given C.
  2. For all ω,ω′∈C with ωJ=ωJ′, we have ω∈A if and only if ω′∈A.
  3. A∩C=(A∩C)J×CJ―.
Moreover, the history ℋ(A∣C) is the smallest set J that disintegrates C and that satisfies A∩C=(A∩C)J×CJ―.

Definition C.6 irrelevant factors, cohistory definition
Paper · arXiv:2412.02579v2

Let A,C⊆Ω, and let (P,Q)∈△C,i⊗(Ω). We say that i∈I is emph(P,Q)-irrelevant to A given C if P(A∣C)=Q(A∣C). A factor i∈I is (globally) irrelevant to A given C, if it is (P,Q)-irrelevant for all (P,Q)∈△C,i⊗(Ω). The cohistory of A given C, denoted Cohistory(A∣C) is the set of all i∈I that are irrelevant to A given C.

Condensation: A Theory of Concepts

Eisenstat (2025) · OpenReview:HwKFJ3odui · Condensation/ · 39 nodes

This formalization is in progress, and no strength classification exists for this paper. It is at milestone M2 — a final statement and a proof for every in-scope node, every declaration axiom-clean — so a card appearing here asserts that the Lean statement shown carries that paper node and is proved; the badge on each declaration (axiom-clean) is the machine-checked confirmation. It is not yet registered as completed: the human statement read-through is outstanding. The legend below the fold says what each badge means and counts both. The paper's scope is settled at 42 numbered nodes; Examples 5.1–5.3 are proposed out of scope pending a ruling. There is no modelling substitution: Condensation.RVModel is Definition 3.1 verbatim, including its "with finite entropy" clause on the sample space. The narrowing dd:finite-range — every random variable of a model has finite range, rather than merely countable discrete range with finite entropy — was disclosed here until 2026-08-17 and was retired that day, when the substrate ShannonInformation/FiniteEntropy/ reached the corpus this development needs; Condensation/KNOWLEDGE.md's disclosures list is empty, and Condensation.Example.geomModel (a geometric variable on ℕ, provably not finite-range) is the witness that the model class genuinely grew. Numbered nodes with no Lean statement annotated to them: Example 5.1, Example 5.2, Example 5.3.

How nodes are cited

This paper numbers its results through a single section-scoped counter shared by every environment — definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, corollaries and examples all draw from it — so node ids read Definition 2.1 through Corollary 5.10, and the printed number is the provenance key. What is different here is the source. This paper has no arXiv record and its LaTeX is not public, so unlike every other paper on this page there is no TeX in the repository to recompute numbers from. The committed source is Condensation/notes/condensation-25-07.txt, a pdftotext -layout extraction of the committed PDF, and scripts/check-condensation-nodes.py reads the printed numbers off its header lines. Because the extraction is therefore itself provenance-bearing, that checker additionally asserts that exactly the paper's 42 nodes are derived, so a re-extraction that mangles a header fails the build instead of quietly shrinking the set of nodes an annotation is allowed to name.

For the same reason the paper statements below are shown verbatim as extracted, in a preformatted block, rather than converted to typeset mathematics as the other four sections are: there is no markup to convert, and reflowing the text would mean rewriting the paper's statement. The extraction keeps the printed line breaks and the alignment of displayed equations, and the extractor's f-ligature slots are resolved back to letters; nothing else is altered. Where a statement is hard to read here, read the committed PDF.

structure RVModel (I : Type w) [Finite I] where
  /-- The sample space `Ω`. -/
  Ω : Type u
  [mΩ : MeasurableSpace Ω]
  [countΩ : Countable Ω]
  [singΩ : MeasurableSingletonClass Ω]
  /-- The probability measure `P` on `Ω`. -/
  P : Measure Ω
  [probP : IsProbabilityMeasure P]
  /-- Definition 3.1's "with finite entropy": the sample space itself has finite entropy. -/
  [finiteEntropy_Ω : ShannonInformation.FiniteEntropyMeasure P]
  /-- The range `Rᵢ` of the `i`-th variable. -/
  R : I → Type v
  [mR : ∀ i, MeasurableSpace (R i)]
  [countR : ∀ i, Countable (R i)]
  [singR : ∀ i, MeasurableSingletonClass (R i)]
  /-- The random variables `Xᵢ : Ω → Rᵢ`. -/
  X : ∀ i, Ω → R i
  measurable_X : ∀ i, Measurable (X i)
  finiteEntropy_X : ∀ i, ShannonInformation.FiniteEntropyOf (X i) P

variable models, π : Ω → Λ and ρ : Λ → Ω are probability-preserving maps, and

    {Λ₁ : Type u₁} [MeasurableSpace Λ₁] (P₁ : Measure Λ₁)
    {Λ₂ : Type u₂} [MeasurableSpace Λ₂] (P₂ : Measure Λ₂)
    (π₁ : Λ₁ → Ω) (π₂ : Λ₂ → Ω) where
  /-- Definition 4.11's hypothesis on the diagram (4.42): `π₁` is probability preserving. -/
  π₁_pres : MeasurePreserving π₁ P₁ PΩ
  /-- Definition 4.11's hypothesis on the diagram (4.42): `π₂` is probability preserving. -/
  π₂_pres : MeasurePreserving π₂ P₂ PΩ
  /-- The amalgamating countable discrete probability space `Λ₀`. -/
  Λ₀ : Type u₀
  [mΛ₀ : MeasurableSpace Λ₀]
  [countΛ₀ : Countable Λ₀]
  [singΛ₀ : MeasurableSingletonClass Λ₀]
  /-- The probability measure `P₀` on `Λ₀`. -/
  P₀ : Measure Λ₀
  [probP₀ : IsProbabilityMeasure P₀]
  /-- The projection `ρ₁ : Λ₀ → Λ₁` of (4.43). -/
  ρ₁ : Λ₀ → Λ₁
  /-- The projection `ρ₂ : Λ₀ → Λ₂` of (4.43). -/
  ρ₂ : Λ₀ → Λ₂
  ρ₁_pres : MeasurePreserving ρ₁ P₀ P₁
  ρ₂_pres : MeasurePreserving ρ₂ P₀ P₂
  /-- The square (4.43) commutes. -/
  comm : π₁ ∘ ρ₁ = π₂ ∘ ρ₂

Condensation.ITree.labelaxiom-cleanCondensation/Quantitative.lean
def label [SemilatticeInf α] : ITree α → α
  | leaf a => a
  | node l r => l.label ⊓ r.label

@[simp] lemma label_leaf [SemilatticeInf α] (a : α) : (leaf a).label = a
Condensation.ITree.intersectionsaxiom-cleanCondensation/Quantitative.lean
def intersections [SemilatticeInf α] : ITree α → List (α × α × α)
  | leaf _ => []
  | node l r => (l.label, r.label, l.label ⊓ r.label) :: (l.intersections ++ r.intersections)

@[simp] lemma intersections_leaf [SemilatticeInf α] (a : α) :
    (leaf a).intersections = []

Proposition 5.7 propositionaxiom-clean
Paper · OpenReview:HwKFJ3odui
Let (V, E) be a directed binary tree, let M be an intersection-
closed collection of sets, and let ℓ̃ be a function from the set of leaves of V to M .
Then, there is a unique extension of ℓe to a function ℓ : V → M such that (V, E, ℓ)
is an intersection tree. That function ℓ assigns to each internal vertex the meet of
all the labels of the leaves which are its ancestors.
